source.title: A2D: Any-Order, Any-Step Safety Alignment for Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Wonje Jeung; Sangyeon Yoon; Yoonjun Cho; Dongjae Jeon; Sang-Woo Shin; Hyesoo Hong; Albert No

record.tranche_reason: Adapts the per-token KL analysis used in the original work to diffusion language models, and reports results on those models and related safety attacks.
record.gate_note: Reports harmfulness outcomes for refusal-trained (RT), benign-data SFT, and A2D models; only benign SFT rows are included for V2. A2D and attack results are included for V4/V7. Other baseline results are omitted. The paper cites prior work on shallow alignment and attacks; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Applies the Qi et al. per-token KL analysis and prefilling attacks to diffusion language models (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream). This is a new architecture setting with its own results on V3 and V4. It also reports benign SFT outcomes (V2) and a token-level deepening method, A2D (V7). The decoding-step setting makes it T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say existing dLLM alignment is shallow, with safety signals decaying after the first decoding steps across orders. Response-level baselines (RT, SFT, VRPO) stay vulnerable to prefilling/DIJA. Token-level [EOS] supervision under random masking (A2D) cuts DIJA from over 80% to near zero with little capability loss, and enables real-time monitoring and early rejection.
record.recipe_differences: Uses diffusion-model per-token KL analysis and evaluates A2D token-level [EOS] training, rather than reproducing the original autoregressive fine-tuning interventions. It additionally tests benign-subset SFT and several jailbreak attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: For the original models, KL decays across left-to-right, confidence-based, and random decoding. A2D’s DIJA results vary by model and decoding strategy; ASR is reported across left-to-right, right-to-left, confidence, entropy, and random strategies. SFT outcomes vary by model and attack.

fits_no_version.finding: [EOS] probability at the first decoding step serves as an early-reject signal (up to 19.3× faster refusals). It also acts as a per-step harmfulness monitor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token-level deep alignment yields an internal harmfulness signal usable for monitoring and early rejection.

record.problems: Per-token KL values are presented in figures without exact numeric values in the text. Table 2 does not state uncertainty estimates. The evaluations use a limited set of three instruction-tuned diffusion models and one named harmfulness dataset for the main results; A2D is an additional alignment intervention, not a comparison isolating which part of its training objective causes the effect.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted RT and VRPO outcome rows and A2D outcomes for Zeroshot, PAIR, and ReNe in Table 1, as they are not needed to record the tested claim versions within the 60-row limit. Also omitted the qualitative examples, capability outcomes, XSTest/OR-Bench compliance, early-rejection timing, and auxiliary benchmark tables because they do not directly measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful compliance examples. RT trains refusals, not harmful answers.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks. LoRA rank 32 is only a training setting.
Does not isolate whether data or objective causes the original models' shallowness.
Dream KL not measured. KL is indexed by diffusion decoding step, not autoregressive position (left-to-right is the AR analogue). KL values are figure-only.
No adversarial suffix (GCG-style) or sampling-parameter attacks.
Only one benign dataset (BeaverTails safe subset) at one size. No dose or dataset variation.

missing.what: Table 2 PAIR and ReNe ASR across five decoding orders, with and without A2D. A2D leaves roughly 8-22% on the LLaDA family.
A2D adapted to autoregressive Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B. Prefilling 47.5→0.0 and 46.3→0.0; original zeroshot 2.5/5.0 vs prefilling 47.5/46.3; PAIR only 42.5→29.4 on LLaMA.
Adaptive [EOS]-interference attacks (Long-Answer, Do-Not-EOS) on A2D. ASR stays low: LLaDA 13.1/12.5, Dream 3.8/1.9.
DIJA on StrongReject, JailbreakBench and AdvBench, Initial vs A2D: 77-92% → 0-1.3%.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 'challenges' label (A2D rows) and V4 'limits_scope' label (A2D results) are misattributed. A2D effects belong to V7. The record's V7 limits_scope on r37/r38 (3.1-3.8% vs about 80%) is not a real limitation and is replaced by the PAIR/ReNe residuals. For V2: the SFT 'safe subset' of BeaverTails likely includes harmful prompts paired with safe responses, which may explain lowered jailbreak ASR. From omitted rows: RT keeps Prefilling at 65.8/66.0 despite Zeroshot 5.0/7.1, consistent with V4. VRPO lowers LLaDA Prefilling to 9.0 but not LLaDA-1.5 (57.3). A2D has a small alignment tax (e.g. LLaDA-1.5 math 46.9→44.8) and no XSTest over-refusal. Dream right-to-left PAIR/ReNe values are decoding artefacts per the authors.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune with harmful examples that teach harmful compliance; RT instead trains full-sequence refusals on harmful prompts.
Tests SFT on the safe subset of BeaverTails, not a broad range of ordinary or carefully selected benign datasets or example counts.
Measures per-token KL along diffusion decoding trajectories, not autoregressive response-token positions.
Tests Prefilling, DIJA, and decoding-order strategies; does not test adversarial suffixes or decoding-parameter changes.
LoRA rank is specified for training, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Proposes randomized masking and token-level supervision as the mechanism for A2D, but does not isolate whether training data or objective causes the original models’ shallow alignment.
Tests A2D’s token-level training and outcomes on the evaluated attacks and models; does not establish whether deepening holds across other architectures or training settings.
